questions.prompt: Which branch of science studies living things like plants, animals and tiny one-celled creatures?
questions.explain: Life science, also called biology, is the study of everything that is alive.

questions.prompt: Which branch of science studies rocks, planets and stars?
questions.explain: Earth science covers our planet and space, including nonliving things like rocks and stars.

questions.prompt: What is a hypothesis?
questions.answer: A prediction that can be tested
wrong: A fact that has been proven forever
A list of materials for an experiment
The final result of an experiment
questions.explain: A hypothesis is an educated guess about what will happen, and you must be able to test it.

questions.prompt: What do scientists use to make observations?
questions.explain: Observing means using your senses, often helped by tools like rulers and thermometers, to describe what happens.

questions.prompt: Every measurement needs a number and what else?
questions.explain: "5" alone means nothing. "5 meters" or "5 minutes" tells you what was measured.

questions.prompt: What is the conclusion of a scientific investigation?
questions.answer: What you found out from the investigation
questions.explain: The conclusion sums up your findings and says whether they matched your hypothesis.

questions.prompt: What is a scientific model?
questions.answer: A simpler representation of something real
wrong: A perfect copy that is never wrong
A rule that can never change
questions.explain: Models help us study things that are too big, too small or too costly to look at directly.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a quantitative observation?
questions.explain: Quantitative observations use numbers and measurements. Color, smell and feel are qualities.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a qualitative observation?
wrong: The rock has a mass of 40 g
There are 3 rocks in the jar
questions.explain: Qualitative observations describe qualities like texture, color or smell instead of numbers.

questions.prompt: What usually comes first in a scientific investigation?
questions.explain: Science starts with a question about how the world works. Research, testing and conclusions come after.

questions.prompt: After you make a hypothesis, what is the next step?
questions.answer: Test it with experiments and observations
wrong: Announce it as a proven fact
questions.explain: A hypothesis is only useful once you test it and compare the results with your prediction.

questions.prompt: Your results do not support your hypothesis. What should you do?
questions.answer: Make a new hypothesis and test again
wrong: Change the data so it matches
Say the hypothesis was right anyway
questions.explain: Scientists use what they learned to form a better hypothesis and start the process again.

questions.prompt: A globe is an example of which kind of model?
questions.explain: A globe is a real object you can hold that represents Earth, so it is a physical model.

questions.prompt: What can evidence from experiments do to a hypothesis?
questions.answer: Support it or go against it
wrong: Turn it into a law right away
questions.explain: Evidence, like observations and data, can back up a hypothesis or show it is wrong.

questions.prompt: What is the main difference between a scientific law and a scientific theory?
questions.answer: A law describes what happens; a theory explains why
wrong: A law is a guess; a theory is a fact
A theory is untested; a law is tested
A law is about living things only
questions.explain: Both are based on many observations. A law tells what nature does, and a theory explains the reason.

questions.prompt: Which best describes a scientific theory?
questions.answer: A well-tested explanation backed by many observations
wrong: A wild guess with no evidence
The result of one single experiment
A prediction nobody has tested yet
questions.explain: In science, a theory is not just a hunch. It has been tested again and again for a long time.

questions.prompt: Newton's law of universal gravitation predicts how objects fall. Why is it called a law?
questions.answer: It describes how objects behave under gravity
wrong: It explains exactly why gravity exists
It was never tested by anyone
It only works on falling apples
questions.explain: A law describes a pattern in nature very reliably, even if it doesn't explain why the pattern happens.

questions.prompt: A shop owner uses an equation of last year's costs to predict next year's costs. What kind of model is this?
questions.explain: Equations and number patterns that predict things are mathematical models.

questions.prompt: A program that shows how a storm might move across a map over the next week is what kind of model?
questions.explain: Simulations that run on a computer, like weather forecasts, are computer models.

questions.prompt: An experiment's results don't match the prediction. Was the experiment a waste?
questions.answer: No, learning what is false helps find what is true
wrong: Yes, it must be thrown away
Yes, it means the scientist failed
No, because the data can be changed
questions.explain: A wrong prediction still teaches you something and points you toward a better idea.

questions.prompt: A scientist studies how iron and oxygen join to form rust. Which field of science is this?
questions.explain: Chemistry is the part of physical science that studies matter and how it changes into new substances.
